passages.t: Dead, made alive: ‘by grace you have been saved’
passages.happening:
Paul tells the readers' story in three steps.

Where they were. “And you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air” (verses 1-2). And not only them: “All of us also lived among them at one time” (verse 3).

What God did. “But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved!” (verses 4-5). God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him (verse 6), to show “the surpassing riches of His grace” (verse 7).

What it means. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (verses 8-9). “For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
‘Dead’ is a strong word. Paul does not say they were sick and needed help. He says they were dead toward God, unable to give themselves life. That is why the rescue had to be God's.

Three forces held them: ‘the ways of this world’, the habits and values of a society without God; ‘the ruler of the power of the air’, the devil, whom many in that world pictured as ruling the unseen spaces between earth and heaven; and ‘the cravings of our flesh’, desires turned in on themselves. Outside pressure, an enemy, and our own hearts.

Notice that Paul says ‘all of us’. He, a Jew who had kept the law, puts himself in the same place as the Gentiles. ‘Children of wrath’ means people who stood under God's just judgment on sin. No one stood outside it.

Then the two most important words in the passage: ‘But God’. Everything turns on him. His love, his mercy, his grace. He made us alive, raised us, seated us with Christ. In the Greek these verbs are all ‘with’ verbs: made alive with, raised with, seated with. Believers share what happened to Jesus.

‘Workmanship’ is the word for something made, a work of art or craft. Believers are God's handiwork. And the good works come after, not before: we are not saved by them, but saved for them.
passages.ot:
The prophets pictured God giving life to the dead. Ezekiel saw a valley of dry bones and heard God say, “I will put My Spirit in you and you will live” (Ezekiel 37:14).

God's rich mercy is the God who revealed himself to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

And the warning against boasting is old. Moses told Israel not to say, “Because of my righteousness the LORD has brought me in to possess this land” (Deuteronomy 9:4).
passages.hard:
If we are saved ‘not by works’, why does verse 10 speak of good works? And how does this fit with James, who says that faith without works is dead (James 2:17)?

All Christians agree on the heart of these verses. Salvation is God's gift, by his grace. No one earns it. No one can boast. And those God saves are made for a new life of good works, which God himself prepared.

Churches describe the link between faith, grace and works in different words. Protestant churches have taught that people are justified by faith alone, and that good works always follow as the fruit of a living faith, though they are never the ground of God's acceptance. The Catholic Church teaches that grace comes first and is never earned, and that by grace a person is truly changed, so that good works done in grace are part of the Christian life God rewards. The Orthodox churches speak of salvation as a gift that heals and transforms the whole person. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint statement agreeing that ‘by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God’, while naming differences that remain. These notes do not choose between them. The book page on Romans sets them out more fully.

As for James, many readers think he and Paul are answering different questions. Paul says works cannot earn salvation. James says that faith which never acts is not real faith. Ephesians 2:10 holds both together: saved by grace, for good works.

What does ‘this’ refer to in verse 8, ‘and this not from yourselves’? In Greek the word does not match ‘faith’ or ‘grace’ exactly. Many readers think it means the whole of salvation by grace through faith. Others think faith itself is meant as God's gift. Either way, the point is the same: none of it starts with us.
passages.asks: Paul says we were dead, and God made us alive. Ask whether you still live as if you must keep yourself alive spiritually by effort. And ask what good works God might have prepared for you, not to earn his love, but because you already have it.

passages.t: The wall torn down: one new people, one household
passages.happening:
Paul asks the Gentile readers to remember where they once stood. They were called ‘uncircumcised’, and “at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world” (verse 12).

“But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ” (verse 13).

“For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility” (verse 14). He did it by abolishing in his flesh “the law of commandments and decrees”, to create “one new man out of the two” (verse 15), reconciling both to God in one body through the cross (verse 16). He came and preached peace to those far and near (verse 17), so that through him “we both have access to the Father by one Spirit” (verse 18).

So the Gentiles are “no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (verse 19), built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone (verse 20). The whole building is growing into “a holy temple in the Lord” (verse 21), “a dwelling place for God in His Spirit” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Notice what Paul says the Gentiles lacked. Not Rome, not Greek learning. They lacked Israel: Israel's Messiah, Israel's covenants, Israel's hope, Israel's God. Being far off meant being far from Israel. Being brought near means being brought into Israel's hope through Israel's Messiah.

‘The dividing wall’ may recall something every Jew in Jerusalem knew. In the temple courts a stone barrier marked how far Gentiles could go. Notices in Greek and Latin warned that a foreigner who went further would be to blame for his own death. One of these stones was found complete in 1871. Paul himself was later attacked in the temple because people thought he had brought a Gentile past that line (Acts 21:28-29). Whether or not Paul had that barrier in mind, his readers would understand the picture: a wall that kept people apart, and the hostility that grew around it.

Christ, Paul says, is ‘our peace’. He does not only bring peace; he is it. In his own body on the cross he made the two groups one, and brought both to God.

‘One new man’ means one new humanity. Not Gentiles turned into Jews, nor Jews turned into Gentiles, but both made new in Christ, with their differences still there but no longer a wall.

A cornerstone was the first stone laid, the one that set the line for the whole building. Christ sets the line for the church. And the building is a temple, the place where God lives. In a city famous for its temple of Artemis, Paul says God's temple is a people.
passages.ot:
Paul echoes Isaiah: “Peace, peace to those far and near,” says the LORD (Isaiah 57:19). In Isaiah the words were for scattered Israel. Paul hears in them Gentiles, far off, and Jews, near, both brought to God.

The cornerstone comes from Isaiah too: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation” (Isaiah 28:16). And from the psalm Jesus quoted: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22).

God had always promised to live among his people: “I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God” (Exodus 29:45). Paul says that promise now takes shape in a people from every nation.
passages.hard:
What does it mean that Christ abolished ‘the law of commandments and decrees’? And is this a word against the Jewish people?

First, what it cannot mean. Paul does not say that the law was evil, or that the Jewish people are rejected. In this very passage the great gift Gentiles receive is to share in Israel's covenants and hope. Elsewhere Paul says, “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12), and that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1).

Readers explain ‘abolishing’ in more than one way. Many think Paul means the law in its role as a wall: the commands, such as circumcision and the food laws, that marked Israel off from the nations. In Christ these no longer divide. Others think he means the law as a whole covenant, fulfilled in Christ, so that both Jews and Gentiles now come to God by the same way. Many hold that the law's moral heart still stands, summed up in love (Romans 13:8-10). These notes do not choose.

What all readings agree on is that the wall Christ broke down was hostility, not a people. The point of the passage is peace between Jews and Gentiles, and both brought to God. For centuries some Christians used words from the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.
passages.asks: Christ tore down the wall of hostility. Ask what walls still stand in your life or your church: between races, classes, political sides, old and young. Ask which side of the wall you are on, and whether you have helped keep it up. And if Christ is our peace, ask who you need to make peace with.
